canonical_statement: The study evaluates whether bidirectionally coupling hierarchical planning with episodic memory improves long-horizon software issue resolution by LLM agents.
The evaluation addresses effectiveness, trajectory mechanism, generality across models/frameworks/tasks, and whether coupled planning and memory outperform either component alone.
The primary evaluation population is the 500 human-validated issues in SWE-bench Verified.
The harness-matched baseline is the mini-SWE-agent loop with PMCoder planning, episodic memory, injection, and execution-grounding components disabled.
PMCoder augments the repository-level observe-act loop with a hierarchical phase planner, episodic memory, tool-result state injection, and execution-grounded verification updates.

exposures.details: hierarchical phase planner + episodic memory + tool-result injection + execution grounding

canonical_statement: A SWE-bench Verified instance is resolved only when the submitted patch passes the official fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests; errored runs and non-applicable patches count as unresolved.

outcome.definition: Submitted patch passes official fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests

canonical_statement: PMCoder couples plan and memory bidirectionally: current phase and active sub-task guide memory retrieval, while memory-derived trajectory statistics drive stuck detection and replanning.
The hierarchical planner uses four ordered progress phases—exploration, hypothesis, implementation, and verification—plus a backtrack recovery event outside the ordering.
One start-of-task LLM call decomposes the issue into typed phase-tagged sub-tasks; per-step phase detection, bookkeeping, backtracking, and replanning are deterministic.

Per-step phase detection uses ordered rules over shell-command behavior and stated reasoning; forward moves can occur immediately, whereas backward or lateral moves require repeated evidence through hysteresis.
After a minimum-step floor, stuck detection can be triggered by persistent nonzero returns, excessive repeated edits to one file, read saturation without edits, or repeated normalized actions.
When backtracking triggers, the planner marks the active sub-task failed and pushes bounded recovery sub-tasks onto a goal stack, including a revert-then-refix recovery path.
A terminal verification sub-task completes only after a successful verification step using the execution-grounded completion predicate.
At each step the planner exports phase, active sub-task, progress counts, most-touched files, a phase token budget, and a backtrack flag; this signal conditions memory retrieval.

Each episodic-memory node stores episode text plus message role, recency identifier, compressed content, summary, edit metadata, and files touched; observation edit metadata is derived from the executed command.
The memory graph stores raw observations only; injected context alters the live conversation but is not re-ingested into the graph.
Memory retrieval uses a token-budgeted maximal-marginal-relevance beam search that always retains the task statement, recent tail, and an anchor seeded from active sub-task keywords.
Candidate retrieval gain is scored as λ·relevance minus (1−λ) times maximum similarity to already selected nodes, with similarity defined by IDF-weighted Jaccard overlap.

Retrieval relevance combines an IDF-weighted lexical score with proximity in an incrementally built code-structure graph containing same-file co-occurrence, Python import, and trajectory-adjacency edges.

Retrieval policy is phase-conditioned: exploration and backtracking retrieve broadly with larger diversity-oriented budgets, whereas implementation uses a smaller graph-weighted budget focused on the edit site.
PMCoder leaves message history unchanged and appends a marker-delimited plan-and-memory block to the most recent tool-result message to preserve tool-call/tool-result pairing.
Plan-memory injection occurs only when plan state changes, and a novelty filter suppresses already surfaced memory nodes in favor of short prescriptive signals.

For instances with a validated issue-reproduction script, the grounding layer reruns the script after file-mutating edits and marks the verdict pass when the issue no longer reproduces and fail when it still does.
The reproduction verdict is advisory to the model and also updates internal plan state; a terminal verification sub-task cannot complete while the latest verdict remains fail.
After a Python-file edit, a compile check can flag an unparsable edit; recovery can restore heavily edited files to the committed state before re-examining and re-fixing the failure.
The four explicit couplings are phase-to-retrieval, sub-task-to-retrieval, memory-statistics-to-plan, and reproduction-verdict-to-plan.

The headline configuration serves Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 with vLLM and LiteLLM tool calls at temperature 0.0, a 65,536-token context cap, 250 assistant-turn step budget, and $3.0 per-instance cost cap.
Default PMCoder retrieval uses MMR λ=0.7, lexical/graph relevance weights 0.5/0.5, a 16k-token memory budget, and a 4k-character cap per memory node.
Default phase budgets are 20k/16k/12k/16k/20k tokens for exploration/hypothesis/implementation/verification/backtrack, with 2-step phase hysteresis.

Default recovery thresholds include minimum backtrack step 10, cooldown 8 steps, goal-stack depth 16, failed-return threshold 5, repeated-edit threshold 6, read-saturation threshold 15, and repeated-action threshold 8.
Execution grounding allows at most four reproduction checks per episode with a 180-second timeout per check.
Issue-reproduction scripts are extracted offline from issue text alone by the same Qwen3-Coder model; the extraction prompt does not expose the gold patch or hidden tests.

A candidate reproduction script is admitted only if it reproduces the pre-edit failure on the unmodified repository within the configured timeout; otherwise the verdict is undefined and PMCoder uses the ungated completion predicate.
The headline Qwen comparison and component ablation use three runs per arm because FP8 serving is not bit-reproducible even at temperature 0.
The primary repeated-run uncertainty analysis uses an instance-level cluster bootstrap over paired resolved indicators; paired McNemar tests are used as a complementary test.
The component ablation uses a run-level balanced 2×2 factorial model with planning, memory, and their interaction as fixed effects.
Across three Qwen3-Coder runs, PMCoder resolved a mean 167.3/500 issues (33.5%) versus 142.3/500 (28.5%) for baseline, an improvement of 25.0 resolved instances (+5.0 percentage points).
The three Qwen3-Coder PMCoder runs resolved 170, 164, and 168 instances, while baseline resolved 139, 144, and 144.
Each of the three trial-paired McNemar tests for the headline Qwen comparison was significant, with p values between 0.002 and 0.033.
In the <15 min human fix-time tier, baseline resolved 89/194 and PMCoder resolved 101/194, a difference of 12 instances (+6.2 percentage points).
In the 15 min–1 h human fix-time tier, baseline resolved 50/261 and PMCoder resolved 67/261, a difference of 17 instances (+6.5 percentage points).
In the 1–4 h human fix-time tier, baseline resolved 0/42 and PMCoder resolved 2/42, a difference of 2 instances.
In the >4 h human fix-time tier, baseline resolved 0/3 and PMCoder resolved 0/3, a difference of 0 instances.
PMCoder reduced failed-action recurrence rate from 0.0137 to 0.0069, a PMCoder/baseline ratio of 0.50×.

In the OpenHands framework port with Qwen on Verified-500, PMCoder resolved 169/500 (33.8%) versus 146/500 (29.2%) for OpenHands baseline, a gain of 23 cases (+4.6 percentage points).

canonical_statement: The authors interpret the improvement as primarily reducing state-management failures within the base model’s capability frontier rather than increasing the base model’s reasoning ability.

PMCoder adds one LLM call per episode for initial decomposition; per-step planning is deterministic, memory retrieval uses no model call, and execution grounding adds at most four cached timeout-bounded script runs per episode.
The same Qwen3-Coder model is used both to extract issue-reproduction scripts and to run the headline agent, so residual script errors may affect grounding-specific mechanism analyses.

The FP8 Qwen endpoint is not bit-reproducible even at temperature 0; Qwen headline and ablation results are repeated three times, while Claude, DeepSeek, OpenHands, and TerminalWorld generality probes are single runs.
PMCoder thresholds and budgets were fixed from pilot runs before the final Verified-500 evaluations rather than tuned on final headline resolved counts.
SWE-bench Verified resolved status is an operational proxy for issue resolution, and a patch can pass held-out tests while diverging from maintainer intent.
The RQ4 ablation isolates planning and memory under the fixed scaffold but does not separately estimate the contributions of execution grounding or edit-integrity recovery.
The headline evidence is from SWE-bench Verified-500 and one open-weight 30B model; transfer to other languages and private codebases remains untested.
Cross-model, OpenHands, and TerminalWorld evaluations are supporting generality probes and do not establish a universal SWE-agent ranking.
The paper reports an anonymized implementation and replication package at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21035632.
The authors conclude that long-horizon repair benefits from planning and memory being designed as a coupled state system, with execution evidence helping keep the shared state reliable.
